subtitle: Building new columns from the ones you already have.

eyebrow: A new column from a vectorized operation
code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
df["line_total"] = df["quantity"] * df["unit_price"]
print(df[["order_id", "quantity", "unit_price", "line_total"]].head())
caption: No loop, no .apply() needed. Pandas multiplies the whole column at once — faster and more concise, always preferred for simple arithmetic.

eyebrow: .apply() with a lambda, for logic arithmetic can't express
code:
df["order_size"] = df["line_total"].apply(
    lambda total: "Large" if total >= 200 else "Standard"
)
print(df["order_size"].value_counts())

# Standard    14
# Large        6
caption: "Large if >= $200, else Standard" isn't a single arithmetic expression — it's a conditional, so .apply() is the right tool.
clip(lower=0) replaces any value below 0 with 0. It doesn't retroactively fix line_total — order of operations matters.

eyebrow: The .str accessor: string ops across a whole column
caption: .str exposes ordinary string methods across an entire column at once — the vectorized equivalent of looping and calling .upper().
